title: Why Won’t Beijing Step On The Gas?
gist: China holds the world's cheapest cost of capital, labor and electricity plus decades-built infrastructure (top rail network, six of the world's top 10 ports), yet auto sales, retail sales, PMIs and housing starts have all underwhelmed recently — a supply/demand mismatch framed as 'why won't Beijing step on the gas.'

insights.claim: China currently has the world's cheapest cost of capital, the cheapest cost of labor when adjusted for productivity, and the cheapest cost of electricity of any major economy.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: These input-cost advantages should make China highly competitive for investment and production, sharpening the puzzle of why growth remains weak despite them.
insights.quote: China today benefits from the cheapest cost of capital in the world, the cheapest cost of labor (at least when adjusted for productivity—see Unraveling China’s Productivity Paradox) and the cheapest cost of electricity.
insights.locator: Why Won't Beijing Step On The Gas?

insights.claim: China's cheap-labor advantage is only true once wages are adjusted for productivity, a point the author flags by pointing readers to a companion piece, 'Unraveling China's Productivity Paradox,' as the deeper explanatory factor.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Investors comparing China's competitiveness to other economies should track productivity trends, not just headline wage levels, since the productivity adjustment is doing the heavy lifting in the cost comparison.
insights.quote: the cheapest cost of labor (at least when adjusted for productivity—see Unraveling China’s Productivity Paradox)
insights.locator: Why Won't Beijing Step On The Gas?

insights.claim: Over the past three decades China has built the world's most complete rail network, an extensive highway system, clean and efficient subways in almost all major cities, and now hosts six of the world's ten largest ports.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: This infrastructure base is sunk capital that should support logistics efficiency and industrial output, making the current growth slowdown hard to explain by physical supply-side constraints.
insights.quote: The country has also spent the past three decades building up domestic infrastructure... today China enjoys the world’s most complete rail network, an impressive system of highways, clean and efficient subways in almost all major cities, six of the top 10 largest ports in the world
insights.locator: China today benefits from the cheapest cost of capital

themes.theme: The growth paradox: strong supply side, weak macro data

insights.claim: Despite China's cost advantages and world-class infrastructure, the economy has not been growing strongly and has instead disappointed relative to what its structural strengths would imply.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: The mismatch between supply-side strengths and weak demand-side data points to the constraint being something other than physical capacity or input costs — the article's central puzzle for why Beijing hasn't stimulated harder.
insights.quote: On paper, the Chinese economy should thus be growing gangbusters. But obviously, this has not been the case; quite the contrary.
insights.locator: On paper, the Chinese economy should thus be growing gangbusters

insights.claim: In recent months nearly all major Chinese macro indicators — auto sales, retail sales, manufacturing PMIs, and housing starts — have come in below expectations.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Broad-based weakness spanning consumption, manufacturing sentiment, and housing signals a demand-side problem rather than a sector-specific one, relevant for calibrating expectations around Chinese stimulus and growth reacceleration.
insights.quote: In recent months, almost all Chinese macro data point releases, whether auto sales, retail sales, PMIs, housing starts… have underwhelmed.
insights.locator: In recent months, almost all Chinese macro data

insights.claim: The article's framing — asking why Beijing 'won't step on the gas' despite having cheap capital, labor and electricity plus top-tier infrastructure — implies the growth shortfall is a matter of policy choice or willingness to stimulate, not a lack of capacity or resources.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: If the binding constraint is policy willingness rather than physical or cost bottlenecks, investors should watch Beijing's fiscal/monetary stimulus signals as the swing factor for a China growth reacceleration, not input-cost or infrastructure data.
insights.locator: Why Won't Beijing Step On The Gas?
